- How Duolingo Turned a Free Language App Into a $7.7B Business | WSJ The Economics Of: Kind: captions Language: en (upbeat music) - [Reporter] This is Duolingo. Around 34 million people use the language learning app every single day, some for well over a decade, making the company around $500 million annually and making it one of the top education apps in Apple's App Store for the past decade. And yet. - Most people who use Duolingo do not pay. - [Reporter] All of its lessons are completely free to access. Only around 9% of its users pay and less than 8% of its revenue comes from advertising. So, how does a free educational app manage to also have a valuation of $7.7 billion? And is the company's strategy sustainable? The answer lies in AI, A/B testing, and this little green owl. This is the economics of Duolingo. (phone pings) If you've ever used Duolingo, you'll have noticed it's less like a traditional language lesson and a lot more like a game. Users have lives. Get five answers wrong in a day and you'll run out of lives for that day. Lessons have progress bars and are laid out in a journey. Players gain experience points and streaks encourage users to play every day. The company says that's part of what helped attract some three million users within the first few years. - When we launched, we had a thing that was mobile, free, and fun, and because of that, very quickly it overtook all methods to learn languages. - [Reporter] But before long, Duolingo ran into an issue with its mission to try and deliver free language lessons. - One of our board members who had just invested in Duolingo, she said, "Look, you can't continue doing this. You gotta make revenue." - We had not given ourselves permission to make any money from our app. It's hard to build up new capabilities in an organization. - We were in a bit of a pickle because we wanted Duolingo to be a free way to learn languages. - [Reporter] So, in 2017, the company introduced advertising, which now accounts for under 8% of its revenue. It also launched a subscription tier where users could pay $10 a month to remove ads and get unlimited lives. The company went public in the summer of 2021 and saw a boom during the pandemic as users practiced languages while travel was limited. Today, analysts say Duolingo is around 12 times bigger than its main rival Babble by downloads with some eight million users who are now paying for the app. And while that's only a small fraction of its overall user base. - The majority of the money is made from this, you know, under 10% of the active users. They give us about 80% of our revenue. - [Reporter] But while Duolingo's growth through gamification and subscriptions may seem pretty simple, there's a lot more going on behind the curtain. Every move the company makes is meticulously crafted down to the pixel, tested on unknown users, and refined using AI, rigorous A/B testing, and constant tweaks to its app. - Whenever people are using the app, we measure how long they use it for, do they come back the next day, et cetera. And we try a lot of things. We try, when do we send you a notification, what we say in the notification? Do we make the lessons a little harder? Do we make them a little easier, a little longer, a little shorter? - [Reporter] Take Duolingo's push notifications. If you forget to do your lessons and risk ending your streak, you'll get a little notification from Duo, the company's mascot, reminding you to return to the app. The messages on the push notifications started out simple enough, but quickly evolved to become the stuff of memes, (bright music) including one particularly effective guilt trip. - We decided that the last notification we would send you was telling you, "Hey, these notifications don't seem to be working. We're gonna stop sending them for now." Sending that got people to come back a lot because they felt guilty. It's like your mother telling you like, "Okay, well, I'll stop, like, guilt tripping you." - [Reporter] Duolingo says that this led to a 3% rise in retention. But crucially, the messages that you receive aren't the same as everybody else's. - AI is used to start figuring out basically, like, which ones of these are more effective for particular users or at particular times of day or whatever and letting the more effective ones rise to the top and then get sent to more people. - [Reporter] To figure out which messages work best, Duolingo built something called a bandit algorithm, named after a reference to a one-armed bandit, a term for a slot machine in a casino. - Say there are, you know, several different slot machines. In this case, think of them as several different notifications we might send people. And we've tried each one some number of times and seen what it paid out each time. So, we have limited information about all these different options. And so the algorithm has to figure out, do I just go back to the one that has so far given me the most money and just go back to that one every time? Or how do I balance that with exploring different options to see maybe they're actually better, but I just got a little unlucky earlier? And each time we send out a notification, we track, did it work? Basically, did they come back to Duolingo, do their daily practice? - [Reporter] For example, the algorithm found out that the notification time for the language you're learning worked better on Chinese learners than English learners. - It's mostly chosen by AI. We must have about a hundred different things that we can send you. They're written by people who are pretty funny and some of them are also written by AI. - [Reporter] And that could be part of the secret to Duolingo's success. The company gets so much data back from those attempting its free lessons that it has a huge database of information that it can feed to its AI algorithms. - They do something like 13 billion exercises every week. We are throwing all that data to AI and using that to personalize the learning experience for everyone to make sure people are learning effectively and staying engaged. - [Reporter] At any given moment, the company is running hundreds of A/B tests like these where one user is given a different experience to another to see which one wins out. Some of the tests are AI powered, others aren't. And for most tests, around 5% of its user base act as unknowing guinea pigs. - I don't know how many A/B tests we've run at this point. It's probably more than 10,000. We've A/B tested our way into getting more people to pay us, into getting more people to use Duolingo, more people to recommend it to their friends, et cetera. So, without having run those, we would not be a successful company. I'm certain of that. - [Reporter] So, if Duolingo's algorithms and A/B testing mean that the company knows exactly what makes its users tick, why are subscriptions only at 8%, and could they be higher? After all, while the company may have 12 times more downloads than Babble, analysts say its revenue is only two to three times that of its rival. - We could tomorrow massively increase the fraction of subscribers by doing certain things. For example, right now, you get one ad at the end of a lesson. We could play five ads That would get a lot more people to subscribe. We could maybe even force people to subscribe. And it is true, we would have an amazing next quarter. However, that would also stifle our growth. - [Reporter] But analysts say that while Duolingo's leading market position may have been achieved by giving away much of its lessons for free, that growth strategy may start to slow, especially as some users leave the app after mastering a language or giving up on it. And that may lead to Duolingo trying to increase the number of paying customers. So, the company is exploring some new ways to get users to part with their cash. It's new AI-powered Duolingo Max tier costs around $30 a month and allows players to role play with AI-powered bots, something the company had previously tried to offer with humans. - We would say, "Okay, so you're telling me that if you could, on Duolingo, press a button and you could have another human on the other side, be able to practice, you would use it?" We'd say, "Okay, do you want to do it right now?" 100% of people would say, "No, no, no, not right now." What I love about AI is that people don't feel like the AI is judging them, even though it actually is judging them. But who cares, right? It's an AI. It's not another human. - [Reporter] But for now at least, Duolingo says it will continue giving away most of its product for free. (gentle music)

The proximity principle is intentionally placing yourself around people and environments that make you think bigger, move faster, and get you closer to your goal. In Kent's journey, when we think about something like Shark Tank, it's very easy to look at it as a play for attention. And yes, obviously that's part of it. And I think sometimes we overcomplicate proximity because I think we think that it has to be reaching out to someone who is 10 steps ahead of us. But in reality, it might just be finding people who are two steps ahead of you, people who are like a little bit further along, who have maybe figured out something that you're currently trying to figure out in that moment. And I think that's what leading with values actually looks like. If you watch the episode, the way that they knew that that wasn't going to work for them when they got that offer, they were very firm on those values that it made that decision almost easy to make. It's being able to make decisions from them when there's something on the table that looks really good on paper but doesn't actually align with where you want to go. Proximity can put you in the right rooms. Attention can get people to see you. Data can tell you what's working. But values are what guide your decisions once you have all of that. And I know that values is a very fluffy principle, but ultimately it's one of the most important things that you solidify early on in your dream. So I think the real question is not just what do you want to build, but it's how do you want to build it and what are the things that you are not willing to compromise on along the way? Which leads us to our next principle to ask for help. And in this one, it sounds incredibly simple, but I actually do think it's one of the hardest to do, especially when you're early on. That if we're capable, if we are smart enough, if we really want this, that we should be able to do it without needing anyone else. And that one decision that not only helped them get through that moment, it ended up leading to a relationship and a partnership down the line. And I think that's such an important shift to understand. I think this ties really closely to the proximity principle because it's one thing to be around the right people, but I actually do think it's another thing to engage with them, to ask questions, to be curious, to not pretend like you have everything figured out. The truth is, there are people who have already solved the problems that you're currently facing. And if you're willing to ask, you can shortcut so much of that learning curve. And I know it's uncomfortable. It literally feels like you're exposing yourself and what you don't know. The core distinction between GDP and the S&P 500 lies in selection bias and structural evolution. While an aggregate economic growth rate (e.g., 4%) reflects the total output of all entities—including stagnant and failing businesses—equity indices like the S&P 500 represent a curated elite. The index outperforms the broader economy through three primary mechanisms: Survivor Bias: Unlike the general economy, which must carry the weight of underperforming sectors, the S&P 500 is a "success-only" club. It aggregates the winners while ignoring the friction of the losers. Semi-Annual Reconstitution: The index effectively "self-cleans" every six months. By rotating out decaying companies and replacing them with high-growth leaders, the S&P 500 maintains a structural momentum that the broader GDP cannot replicate. Global Scalability: The largest 500 companies are not tethered solely to domestic growth; they capture international market share and leverage economies of scale that far exceed the capabilities of the average local business.Bottom Line: The S&P 500 is not a mirror of the economy; it is a filtered performance vehicle designed to capture the ceiling of corporate growth rather than the floor of the aggregate market.

You know, the audience decides what they want to watch and-and the algorithm is just reflecting that, but of course, we are not in this ideal world, and the audience itself is always kind of shifting and changing who they are and what they like to watch, and so, the algorithm, you can think of as following the audience the algorithm is-is chasing this audience around and trying to reach them. Now, what YouTube doesn't much consider, is that well, the YouTube creators use their content to try to chase the algorithm. So these YouTubers who would love to be creating content about, you know, whatever they're most passionate about in whatever way they also see what's popular on the site and they try to make content that will please the algorithm. And so there's a way in which the content is chasing the algorithm, the algorithm is chasing the audience, and if the content actually manages to catch up with the algorithm, you get a-a kind of perverse situation, in which the algorithm is the content. I mean, what do I mean by that? Just a crazy thought experiment: if YouTube wanted more videos of snails, they could make that happen; they don't actually have to go out and make any snail videos, if they just, you know, promoted videos with snail in the title, tomorrow there's gonna be a whole bunch on the front page and trending and then creators be like, "Oh snails are the new thing!", and they're going to go make a bunch of videos about snails. YouTube would love to believe that-that creators don't care about the algorithm - but they do! It's like the core aspect of how creators decide what content to make. Just as a more, uh, down-to-earth example, I can show you a graph of the length of my videos from 2011, through to today. And what you see is, at the beginning, uh, all of my videos averaged about 2 or 3 minutes in length, but these days, I'm fast approaching an average length of video of 10 minutes. Now, YouTube never came to me and said, "Derek, you have to make longer videos"; all they said was, well videos that are longer and get longer watch time will be promoted more on the site, so, people like myself and, you know, all the other creators who wanted to be seen, we made longer videos. It's just, what we did. Now, we know that the algorithm is always changing; they're always trying to optimize it make it work better, but they also change what it's trying to optimize for. In the beginning it was simple: just views, but they quickly figured out that, of course, like, a 20 minute view is worth a lot more than a 5 second view, so the actual metric should be watch time. And this, uh, was advantageous to people like gamers, because people like to watch people play video games for long periods of time. They also reduced the latency of the algorithm, by which I mean it updates every 10 minutes instead of, say, every day, and that's beneficial for news content and things that are really time-sensitive, and to me as a YouTuber what this means is it's impossible to be an expert on YouTube. If you look at what it takes to become an expert at anything, according to the Nobel prize-winning economist Daniel Kahneman, you need, of course, many, many hours of practice. Effortful, deliberate practice. And on YouTube I would argue we get that. You also need timely feedback, and, again, on YouTube we're given plenty of tools to be able to see how our videos are performing; but, when it comes to a reliable environment - this is an environment in which the rules of the game aren't changing: so you can think of something like chess it's possible to be a chess expert, because in the middle of a game of chess, the rules don't suddenly change on you. Now, on YouTube, that is not true. We are not playing by the same rules the whole time, because the algorithm is constantly changing. And so, that puts us in this position, where it's kind of impossible to be experts, and instead we're a little bit more like [page flips], caged pigeons. Okay, go with me on this. Uh, there was this famous experiment where, you know, pigeons were put in a cage with a lever and if they push the lever then they would get some food, and so they very quickly learned that they needed to push the lever and the food would come out, so that's fine. But in a another part of the experiment they disconnected, the lever from the food output and they just supplied food into the cage, kind of, at random and what did the pigeons do? Well, they started to do the types of behaviors that they were doing when the food appeared, so, if one was preening itself then it would keep preening itself, with the expectation that food was coming, and this one, maybe he was pecking the ground; so, the point being they started to engage in these superstitious behaviors, um, because they had related some sort of cause and effect, but there actually wasn't a cause and effect there, and to me, this partly explains the whole YouTube burnout phenomenon, because you have these creators who are stretching themselves to try to chase that algorithm meanwhile the algorithm is constantly shifting and so you never feel like an expert and never quite know what's going on even though you're constantly trying to relate cause and effect now I can understand why the algorithm has to change. I mean in the early days of YouTube, it was this situation where if you had subscribers you were golden because the next time you uploaded some content then YouTube would show it to all your subscribers it'll get a ton of views YouTube would say "oh this is a popular video", show it to even more people, getting you even more subscribers so the next time you launch another video then it goes to more subscribers more views and it was just this positive feedback loop where you would grow and grow and grow a channel so the rich got richer and small channels stayed small so obviously we needed something to break the cycle and so YouTube started doing some experiments where they would essentially change what was recommended to your audience so they would stop showing some of the content from certain subscribers and they saw what happened to views so they started disconnecting these subscribers from the channel No longer was a subscription like "I want to see every video by this person" it was more of a suggestion that maybe something this person creates is something I might like to see and what YouTube found when they did that was that the number of views on the platform the amount of watch time all rose dramatically so for YouTube to get growth of the site they found that reducing the importance of subscriptions was essential and this kind of makes sense if you think about it I mean if you make one great video, that doesn't necessarily mean that every video you're gonna make is gonna be great so it makes sense for YouTube to step in and play some role in terms of determining what gets shown to which audience members Now, as has been observed by MatPat previously, moving away from subscriptions moves YouTube back to what it was like to sell newspapers on the street you really had to inspire people to buy on the spot you have to serve up really sensational news items. - What makes something go viral? | Dao Nguyen: Kind: captions Language: en Last year, some BuzzFeed employees were scheming to prank their boss, Ze Frank, on his birthday. They decided to put a family of baby goats in his office. (Laughter) Now, BuzzFeed had recently signed on to the Facebook Live experiment, and so naturally, we decided to livestream the whole event on the internet to capture the moment when Ze would walk in and discover livestock in his office. We thought the whole thing would last maybe 10 minutes, and a few hundred company employees would log in for the inside joke. But what happened? Ze kept on getting delayed: he went to get a drink, he was called to a meeting, the meeting ran long, he went to the bathroom. More and more people started logging in to watch the goats. By the time Ze walked in more than 30 minutes later, 90,000 viewers were watching the livestream. Now, our team had a lot of discussion about this video and why it was so successful. It wasn't the biggest live video that we had done to date. The biggest one that we had done involved a fountain of cheese. But it performed so much better than we had expected. What was it about the goats in the office that we didn't anticipate? Now, a reasonable person could have any number of hypotheses. Maybe people love baby animals. Maybe people love office pranks. Maybe people love stories about their bosses or birthday surprises. But our team wasn't really thinking about what the video was about. We were thinking about what the people watching the video were thinking and feeling. We read some of the 82,000 comments that were made during the video, and we hypothesized that they were excited because they were participating in the shared anticipation of something that was about to happen. They were part of a community, just for an instant, and it made them happy. So we decided that we needed to test this hypothesis. What could we do to test this very same thing? The following week, armed with the additional knowledge that food videos are very popular, we dressed two people in hazmat suits and wrapped rubber bands around a watermelon until it exploded. Eight hundred thousand people watched the 690th rubber band explode the watermelon, marking it as the biggest Facebook Live event to date. The question I get most frequently is: How do you make something go viral? The question itself is misplaced; it's not about the something. It's about what the people doing the something, reading or watching -- what are they thinking? Now, most media companies, when they think about metadata, they think about subjects or formats. It's about goats, it's about office pranks, it's about food, it's a list or a video or a quiz, it's 2,000 words long, it's 15 minutes long, it has 23 embedded tweets or 15 images. Now, that kind of metadata is mildly interesting, but it doesn't actually get at what really matters. What if, instead of tagging what articles or videos are about, what if we asked: How is it helping our users do a real job in their lives? Last year, we started a project to formally categorize our content in this way. We called it, "cultural cartography." It formalized an informal practice that we've had for a really long time: don't just think about the subject matter; think also about, and in fact, primarily about, the job that your content is doing for the reader or the viewer. Let me show you the map that we have today. Each bubble is a specific job, and each group of bubbles in a specific color are related jobs. First up: humor. "Makes me laugh." There are so many ways to make somebody laugh. You can be laughing at someone, you could laugh at specific internet humor, you could be laughing at some good, clean, inoffensive dad jokes. "This is me." Identity. People are increasingly using media to explain, "This is who I am. This is my upbringing, this is my culture, this is my fandom, this is my guilty pleasure, and this is how I laugh about myself." "Helps me connect with another person." This is one of the greatest gifts of the internet. It's amazing when you find a piece of media that precisely describes your bond with someone. This is the group of jobs that helps me do something -- helps me settle an argument, helps me learn something about myself or another person, or helps me explain my story. that makes me feel something -- makes me curious or sad or restores my faith in humanity. Many media companies and creators do put themselves in their audiences' shoes. But in the age of social media, we can go much farther. People are connected to each other on Facebook, on Twitter, and they're increasingly using media to have a conversation and to talk to each other. If we can be a part of establishing a deeper connection between two people, then we will have done a real job for these people. Let me give you some examples of how this plays out. This is one of my favorite lists: "32 Memes You Should Send Your Sister Immediately" -- immediately. For example, "When you're going through your sister's stuff, and you hear her coming up the stairs." Absolutely, I've done that. "Watching your sister get in trouble for something that you did and blamed on her." Yes, I've done that as well. This list got three million views. Why is that? Because it did, very well, several jobs: "This is us." "Connect with family." Here are some of the thousands and thousands of comments that sisters sent to each other using this list. Sometimes we discover what jobs do after the fact. This quiz, "Pick an Outfit and We'll Guess Your Exact Age and Height," went very viral: 10 million views. Ten million views. I mean -- did we actually determine the exact age and height of 10 million people? That's incredible. It's incredible. In fact, we didn't. Turns out that this quiz went extremely viral among a group of 55-and-up women -- who were surprised and delighted that BuzzFeed determined that they were 28 and 5'9". "They put me at 34 years younger and seven inches taller. I dress for comfort and do not give a damn what anyone says. Age is a state of mind." This quiz was successful not because it was accurate, but because it allowed these ladies to do a very important job -- the humblebrag. Now, we can even apply this framework to recipes and food. A recipe's normal job is to tell you what to make for dinner or for lunch. And this is how you would normally brainstorm for a recipe: you figure out what ingredients you want to use, what recipe that makes, and then maybe you slap a job on at the end to sell it. But what if we flipped it around and thought about the job first? One brainstorming session involved the job of bonding. So, could we make a recipe that brought people together? This is not a normal brainstorming process at a food publisher. So we know that people like to bake together, and we know that people like to do challenges together, so we decided to come up with a recipe that involved those two things, and we challenged ourselves: Could we get people to say, "Hey, BFF, let's see if we can do this together"? The resulting video was the "Fudgiest Brownies Ever" video. It was enormously successful in every metric possible -- 70 million views. And people said the exact things that we were going after: "Hey, Colette, we need to make these, are you up for a challenge?" "Game on." It did the job that it set out to do, which was to bring people together over baking and chocolate. I'm really excited about the potential for this project. When we talk about this framework with our content creators, they instantly get it, no matter what beat they cover, what country they’re in, or what language they speak. So cultural cartography has helped us massively scale our workforce training. When we talk about this project and this framework with advertisers and brands, they also instantly get it, because advertisers, more often than media companies, understand how important it is to understand the job that their products are doing for customers. But the reason I'm the most excited about this project is because it changes the relationship between media and data. Most media companies think of media as "mine." How many fans do I have? How many followers have I gained? How many views have I gotten? How many unique IDs do I have in my data warehouse? But that misses the true value of data, which is that it's yours. If we can capture in data what really matters to you, and if we can understand more the role that our work plays in your actual life, the better content we can create for you, and the better that we can reach you. Who are you? How did you get there? Where are you going? What do you care about? What can you teach us? That's cultural cartography. Thank you. (Applause)

What would you say is the number one mistake people make when trying to go viral social media? >> Yeah. So people just like sometimes I always like to say everyone thinks they're a great marketer. But the thing with content is there are so many case studies out there of people in your niche that have already gone viral. And what you can do is you can just search up your niche in the Instagram explore page and you can click accounts and you can find like the top 10 to 20 people in your account or like in your niche. You go to their accounts and you basically want to look for videos like we call them outlier videos, but it's basically videos that just get a significantly amount or like a how how should I word this? >> Like a higher amount of views than their average. >> Yes. So like I I do what's called the 5x rule. So I'm like, okay, if it gets 5x views and the accounts followers, that's like a viral video in my mind. So we'll add all of those to a spreadsheet from their page. And then we will write out like the hooks. We'll write out how many views it got, the topic of the video, like the format it was filmed in. Um, and we'll do that for like 10 to 20 videos for each creator, um, for those 10 to 20 creators. So, you're getting a list of like few hundred reels that are like the best performing in your niche. And then you just use the hooks and the topics from those videos in your own content, but make the value your expertise and like your actual actionable valuable advice. And that is what works. In 1988, Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond wrote “The Manual”, or “How To Have A Number One The Easy Way”. They’d had a novelty pop song hit the top of the charts earlier that year, and the Manual -- I've had to plastic-wrap my copy, it's a bit rainy -- was a tongue-in-cheek guide to success in the music industry: how to achieve a number one single with no money and no musical talent. Almost all of it is out of date now, but there’s one section, right at the start, that is as relevant today as the day it was written, and it’s trying to talk the reader out of what they think they want. And it says: “The majority of Number Ones are achieved early on in the artist's public career “and before they have been able to establish reputations and build a solid fan base. “Most artists are never able to recover from having one “and it becomes the millstone around their necks to which all subsequent releases are compared. “Either the artist will be destroyed in their attempt “to prove to the world that there are other facets to their creativity “or they succumb willingly and spend the rest of their lives “as a travelling freak show.” A number one song does not make a career. In fact, it can kill a career: if all you’re known for is doing one thing, all the world will want to see is that one thing. A single popular video does not make you a YouTube star, it makes you the person who stands up and repeats that catchphrase over and over again until everyone’s tired of it. There are people out there who think, just one big hit, that’s all they need, that’s the path to stardom and being set for life. They were wrong thirty years ago, and they’re wrong now. If you’re a one-hit wonder, then it’s not you that’s popular; it’s that one hit. What you need is a steady build, a back catalogue, enough time to learn the skills that you need to survive under the spotlight, to have long-term, sustainable success. If you sit round, with a committee, and you ask “What’s funny? What's good? What's popular? What can we make? “What will people be interested in?”, then you’re already on the wrong track. But you know that idea you had when you were in the shower, or in the pub with friends, or just letting your mind wander on a rainy beach today? That idea might be good. Your brain isn’t indexed so you can say “think of something popular”. Your brain thrives on connections. And it is way more difficult to make those connections when your job depends on it. For me, it took me more than a decade of throwing stuff at the internet, of steadily building up a small following and learning my trade before I found the Things You Might Not Know format, an idea that really worked, an idea that got me a large audience and a chance to actually turn this into something that could support me. By sheer luck, that happened at the point where I’d been working somewhere long enough to build up some savings, so I wouldn’t be completely bankrupt if this new, shiny YouTube idea didn’t work out long-term. There’s a reason that a lot of people who make stuff for online platforms are either kids supported by their parents, or students with a lot of time on their hands, or folks who have the means to support themselves. And even if you are one of the lucky ones, if your project starts bringing in some money, if you’re lucky enough to have the budget to be able to book a last-minute sleeper train ticket and travel to a remote, rain-swept Scottish island because it makes a better background for your video, it could still end at any time. You could get ill, or your audience could get bored. Actually, your audience, they will get bored at some point. There are some folks out there, mostly still teenagers, with millions of people already following them and money rolling in, and they think this is going to last forever. But every band’s second album is difficult, and every TV show starts to lose ratings over time as newer things come along. The internet works the same way. The new stuff doesn’t necessarily have to be better: it just has to be exciting. People like to have both familiarity and novelty, but there’s got to be both. Too much familiarity is boring. Too much novelty is scary. If you don’t strike a balance, if you can’t change with the times, someone else will be ready and willing to take your audience. For almost every creator making stuff for the internet, the work they do is a passion project. So if you’re starting out, you should know: it isn’t going to support you for the first few years, perhaps the first few decades, perhaps ever. And if you are one of the lucky ones, if you’ve made it, it very likely won’t support you for life. I mean, if this is a passion project, you probably won’t care about that. And as long as you know that, as long as you plan for it, that’s fine. But you’ll have seen all the creators, in every genre on YouTube, talking about burnout. So, let's spend some time deep diving into swipeway rate and how we can improve this metric. So, what even is swipeway rate, right? So, it measures how quickly a viewer is swiping away from your short. And if you're a Tik Tok user, if you use Instagram reels or even YouTube shorts, you've you've done the doom scroll, right? Where you're sitting there, you're going through video after video, but YouTube is actually measuring all this data. So if you are presented with a video in front of you, and within like a second you decide, ah, no, this video is not for me, and you swipe away, that is the swipeway rate. So you want a low swipeway rate percentage. If too many people are leaving within the first two to three seconds, YouTube is going to stop pushing that video to the broader YouTube community and your short is not going to pick up any steam. If you have a high swipeway rate, meaning a lot of people are swiping away from your video and not choosing to watch it, you have a very, very low chance of virality. - The Psychology of Going Viral: Kind: captions Language: en What makes a piece of content go viral? Is it timing, luck? Or is there a deeper, almost scientific formula behind the most shared videos, posts, and memes? Every day, billions of pieces of content are uploaded to the internet. Most vanish without a trace. But a select few break through the noise, spreading across platforms, continents, and cultures fast, emotionally, and almost uncontrollably. Viral content behaves like a digital pathogen. It infects our attention, replicates in our minds, and drives us to spread it. And behind this contagious behavior lies a fascinating interplay between psychology, technology, and social dynamics. To understand virality, we need to understand the architecture of attention. At its core, viral content taps into primal human triggers. It evokes emotion, often intensely. Whether it's awe, amusement, anger, or anxiety, content that stirs us gets shared. Not because we're generous with our time, but because emotion makes information sticky. Psychologists call this emotional arousal. When we're emotionally activated, our brain prioritizes memory encoding. It also prompts us to act. And in the case of digital platforms, that means commenting, liking, and sharing. But it's not just any emotion. Research shows that high arousal emotions like excitement, fear, or outrage tend to outperform low arousal ones like sadness or contentment. This is why a shocking headline, a hearttoppping video, or an infuriating tweet spreads faster than a balanced report or a reasoned essay. Virality also plays on identity. When we share something, we're not just distributing information. We're performing. We're curating a version of ourselves for the world to see. A funny meme might show that we're witty. A passionate opinion piece reveals our values. A tech video may say we're forward thinking. This identity signaling makes virality intensely personal. We share not just because the content is good, but because it reflects us, our tribe, our beliefs, our tastes. Then there's the role of novelty. The brain is hardwired to seek out the unexpected. Novelty activates the dopamine system, the same system linked to pleasure, motivation, and reward. When something surprises us, we pay attention. We want more, and we want others to experience it, too. That's why so much viral content feels fresh, even if it's recycled. It frames the familiar in a new way or introduces the new in a context we understand. Think of the ice bucket challenge or the Harlem Shake or that one tweet that somehow sums up your entire worldview in 140 characters. Of course, behind all this lies the machine algorithms. Social media platforms are not passive stages. They're active curators designed to maximize engagement. And engagement is often synonymous with virality. When you watch, like, or share something, the algorithm takes note. If others do the same, it amplifies it. The feedback loop accelerates and suddenly a video uploaded in a basement is being seen by millions. But this raises a paradox. Virality feels organic, yet it's heavily engineered. Creators learn to hack these systems. They optimize thumbnails, use emotionally charged language. Strategically post at peak hours. Some even design content to provoke outrage, not because they believe it, but because they know it spreads. This is where the psychology of virality becomes ethically complex because what's viral isn't always what's true or good or meaningful. Sometimes it's the loudest voice in the room, not the wisest, that gets heard. And that can distort reality, making the fringe seem mainstream, the trivial seem important, the harmful seem acceptable. But virality can also be a force for good. It can amplify unheard voices, spread crucial information, launch revolutions, both social and scientific. A single viral video can raise millions for a cause, change laws, or inspire global movements. The difference lies in intention and awareness. Understanding the psychology of going viral isn't just about chasing views. It's about knowing how our minds and the machines we've built interact. It's about wielding that knowledge responsibly. Because in a world where attention is currency, we are all players in a highstakes game of persuasion. What we choose to share shapes what others see. And what we collectively see shapes the world we live in. So next time something goes viral, ask why this? Why now? And what does it say? Not just about the content, but about us. Because virality isn't just a feature of the internet. It's a mirror. And we're the ones holding it

- Why DUMB Ideas Go Viral — Nietzsche & Psychology: Kind: captions Language: en Picture this. In 2018, teenagers across America started filming themselves biting into laundry detergent pods, literally poisoning themselves for internet fame. Meanwhile, millions of people became convinced the earth was flat despite centuries of scientific proof. And right now, as we speak, there's probably some conspiracy theory spreading faster than wildfire across social media. Here's what's fascinating and terrifying. These weren't isolated incidents of individual stupidity. They were mass movements. Collective madness that swept through entire populations like a virus. Why does this happen? Why do the most ridiculous, shallow, and often dangerous ideas spread like wildfire while profound truths struggle to find an audience? Friedrich Nichze had a brutal answer to this question over a century ago, and it's more relevant today than ever. He wrote, "Madness is rare in individuals, but in groups, parties, nations, and ages, it is the rule." Think about that for a moment. The very act of joining a group makes us more susceptible to madness, not less. The herd doesn't make us wiser. It makes us more prone to collective delusions. But why? What is it about human nature that makes us abandon our individual judgment the moment we join a crowd? The answer lies in what Nichzche called the most dangerous force in human society. Herd morality. Nze made a shocking claim that most people still find uncomfortable. Morality itself is nothing more than a herd instinct. It didn't evolve to help us find truth or make us better people. It evolved to keep us compliant, predictable, and equal. Morality is the herd instinct in the individual, he wrote. In other words, what we call our moral compass is actually just our internal GPS designed to keep us within the safe boundaries of the group. This explains something crucial about viral ideas. They don't succeed because they're true or profound. They succeed because they make us feel like we belong. They give us the warm, fuzzy feeling of being part of something bigger than ourselves. Consider how this plays out in our digital age. The ideas that go viral aren't the ones that challenge us to think deeper or question our assumptions. They're the ones that make us feel smart without having to do any real intellectual work. They're the intellectual equivalent of fast food. Instantly satisfying but nutritionally empty. When someone shares a meme that destroys the opposing political party with a single image, they're not engaging in serious political discourse. They're performing membership in their tribe. They're saying, "Look, I'm one of you. I believe what you believe. I hate what you hate." The content doesn't matter. The tribal signal does. This is why conspiracy theories spread so effectively. They offer their believers a sense of special knowledge of being part of an enlightened minority that sees through the lies everyone else accepts. But paradoxically, they achieve this by creating their own herd. a herd of supposed nonconformists who all think exactly alike. But there's something even deeper at work here. Something that Nze understood about human nature that most of us would rather not face. We're absolutely terrified of standing alone. In the 1950s, psychologist Solomon Ash conducted a series of experiments that revealed just how far this terror extends. He showed people a simple line matching task. Which of lines match the length of a target line? The answer was obvious. A child could get it right. But here's the twist. Ash placed real subjects in rooms with actors who were instructed to give obviously wrong answers. When their turn came, about 75% of real subjects gave the wrong answer at least once. They literally denied the evidence of their own eyes to conform to the group. Nichza saw this psychological weakness as the fundamental barrier to human greatness. He wrote, "He who would learn to fly one day must first learn to stand and walk and run and climb and dance. One cannot fly into flying. Most people never even attempt to stand alone. They never learn to trust their own judgment over the groups. They never develop the psychological muscles needed to think independently. It's simply too scary. And why is it scary? Because throughout human history, being expelled from the group meant death. Our ancestors who were too independent, too questioning, too different. They didn't survive long enough to pass on their genes. We're descended from people who were really, really good at conforming. This ancient programming still runs deep in our modern brains. When we see everyone else believing something, sharing something, laughing at something, our primitive brain screams, "Join in, or be left behind." The result, we don't just tolerate dumb ideas. We actively seek them out. They feel safe. They feel familiar. They feel like home. But Nichze identified an even darker aspect of herd psychology. The positive pleasure we get from attacking anyone who dares to think differently. He called this resentiment, a deep poisonous resentment that the average person feels toward anyone who rises above the crowd. It's not just indifference to excellence, it's active hostility toward it. Think about how this plays out in our current culture. When someone becomes successful, innovative, or simply different, what's the first instinct? To find ways to tear them down, to mock them, to find the character flaw, the hypocrisy, the moment of weakness that proves they're just like everyone else. Social media has weaponized this instinct. The comment sections of any platform are filled with people who seem to take genuine joy in destroying anyone who dares to stand out. The more someone achieves, the more vicious the attacks become. This is why dumb ideas often go viral specifically because they mock intelligence, expertise, or independent thought. They don't just unite people around a shared belief. They unite people around a shared enemy. The elites, the experts, the know-it-alls who think they're better than everyone else. There's a perverse satisfaction in believing that all the smart people are actually stupid, that all the experts are actually wrong, that your common sense is superior to their fancy education. It's the ultimate revenge of the herd against anyone who dares to graze outside the fence. Now, let's dig into the psychological machinery that makes dumb ideas so irresistible. Nobel Prize winner Daniel Conaman discovered something crucial about how our brains work. We're wired to favor ideas that feel easy to process. He called this cognitive ease. The feeling we get when information flows smoothly through our minds without friction. Ideas that are simple, familiar, and repeatedly encountered literally feel more true than complex, novel, or challenging ones. This is why clickbait works so well. Headlines like, "You won't believe what this celebrity did," or "This one weird trick doctors hate," bypass our analytical thinking entirely. They feel easy to process, so our brains interpret them as credible. But there's a second psychological principle at work here that makes the effect even more powerful. Psychologist Robert Keelini identified what he called social proof. Our tendency to look around and copy what others are doing, especially when we're uncertain. When we see thousands of people sharing, liking, or commenting on an idea, our brain performs a simple calculation. If everyone believes it, it must be true. We don't consciously think this, but our unconscious mind treats popularity as a proxy for truth. Put these two principles together. Cognitive ease plus social proof and you get the perfect recipe for viral nonsense. An idea that feels easy to understand and that lots of other people seem to accept will spread through a population like a perfectly designed virus. Your brain doesn't ask, "Is this true?" It asks, "Does this feel right? And do other people think so, too?" If the answer is yes, you're already infected. This explains everything from internet memes to political movements to financial bubbles. The ideas that spread fastest aren't the ones that correspond to reality. They're the ones that correspond to our psychological biases. Here's where things get really interesting. Researchers have discovered that different types of content spread at dramatically different speeds through social networks. And there's a clear pattern. Content that triggers strong emotions spreads much faster than content that simply informs. Anger spreads faster than facts. Humor spreads faster than analysis. Fear spreads faster than reassurance. Outrage spreads faster than nuance. This isn't an accident or a flaw in how social media works. It's a feature of how human psychology works. We're social creatures and sharing emotions is one of the primary ways we bond with each other. When we laugh at the same joke or get angry about the same injustice, we're creating and strengthening social connections. But here's the crucial part. Social media algorithms have learned to exploit these exact psychological vulnerabilities. They're designed to surface content that triggers strong emotional responses because that's what keeps us scrolling, clicking, and sharing. The algorithm doesn't care if the content is true. It cares if it's engaging. This creates a systematic bias toward emotional manipulation over factual accuracy. The problem is that truth often isn't emotional. Reality is often boring, complex, and uncertain. It doesn't give us the emotional high that comes from shared outrage or collective laughter. So what spreads isn't what's true. It's what feels significant. And nothing feels more significant than something that makes us feel strongly and that we can share with others to create a sense of unity. Nze understood this about human nature. He wrote there are no facts only interpretations. He wasn't being a post-modern relativist. He was observing that humans don't really respond to raw information. We respond to stories, emotions, and meanings. The herd amplifies feelings, not facts, because sharing feelings deepens belonging in a way that sharing information never can. When we collectively mock the same target or rage against the same enemy, we're not just exchanging information, we're performing a ritual of tribal bonding. [Music] But here's where Nichzche's insights become genuinely frightening. He wasn't just describing an interesting quirk of human psychology. He was warning about the civilizational consequences of herd thinking. When societies become dominated by herd values, when conformity becomes the highest virtue and independent thought becomes the greatest sin, they inevitably sink into what he called mediocrity. The shest way to corrupt a youth is to instruct him to hold in higher esteem those who think alike than those who think differently. Look around at our current moment. How many of our institutions actively reward independent thinking versus conformity to group opinion? How many of our schools teach students to question popular ideas versus to adopt the correct views? How many of our media outlets encourage genuine debate versus tribal cheerleading? The answer is troubling and it's getting worse. When dumb ideas go viral, they don't just entertain us. They shape policy, influence elections, and determine the direction of entire civilizations. The same psychological mechanisms that make us share memes also make us vote for candidates, support causes, and accept explanations for complex problems. History is littered with societies that collapsed not because they lacked smart people, but because their smart people were silenced by the herd. The Soviet Union had brilliant scientists and thinkers, but they were forced to conform to ideological orthodoxy. Nazi Germany had one of the world's most educated populations, but education became a tool of conformity rather than independent thought. The pattern is always the same. First, independent thinking becomes socially costly. Then, it becomes professionally dangerous. Finally, it becomes literally impossible as the herd takes complete control of information, education, and social rewards. We're not there yet, but we're moving in that direction. And the speed of modern communication makes the process much faster than it used to be. What happens when the collective wisdom of crowds becomes the collective madness of mobs? What happens when the democratization of information becomes the democratization of delusion? These aren't abstract philosophical questions anymore. They're urgent practical problems that will determine the future of human civilization. Resistance is still possible, but it requires something NZ called intellectual courage. The willingness to think thoughts that might isolate you from the crowd. First, you must learn to recognize the physiological signs of herd thinking in yourself. When you feel that rush of righteousness that comes from sharing something that destroys your enemies, pause. When you feel the warm glow of belonging that comes from liking what everyone else likes, question it. When you feel the satisfying click of certainty about complex issues, doubt it. These feelings aren't guides to truth. They're warnings that your herd instincts have been activated. Second, develop what we might call cognitive resistance training. Deliberately seek out ideas that make you uncomfortable, not because they're necessarily true, but because discomfort is often a sign that you're breaking out of your intellectual comfort zone. Force yourself to engage with the strongest versions of arguments you disagree with. Third, practice the art of saying, "I don't know." In a world that rewards quick opinions over careful thought, admitting uncertainty has become a radical act. Most viral ideas succeed because they offer false certainty about complex issues. The antidote is to become comfortable with genuine uncertainty, to prefer honest confusion over confident delusion. Finally, accept the social cost of intellectual independence. Nichza was brutally honest about this. The individual has always had to struggle not to be overwhelmed by the tribe. This struggle never ends. There will always be pressure to conform, to simplify, to go along with the crowd. The herd offers immediate rewards. Belonging, certainty, the satisfaction of being right along with everyone else. Independent thought offers something different, the possibility of genuine understanding, even if it comes with loneliness and doubt. Here's the uncomfortable truth. One NZA would instantly recognize we're not just surrounded by dumb ideas. We're actively creating a world where smart ideas can't survive. Every time we reward what's viral over what's valuable, we train our collective mind to crave intellectual junk food. Every time we flatten complexity into cheap simplicity, we build a culture that can't handle nuance. Every time we choose comforting agreement over challenging contradiction, we dig deeper into what Nichze called the grave of the spirit. The real danger isn't just that individuals believe foolish things. It's that our entire information ecosystem is evolving to produce and reward foolishness. Algorithms amplify our worst impulses and mute our best. Think about what this means for the next generation. Children aren't just bumping into bad ideas here and there. They're growing up inside systems that systematically rewire their minds, exploiting the very weaknesses Nichzche warned us about. He put it starkly. What does not kill me makes me stronger. But he also hinted at the flip side. What makes us comfortable makes us weak. And we've built a world designed to keep us as comfortable as possible. The result, a kind of intellectual diabetes. We've gorged on so much mental sugar, we've lost the ability to process real nutrition. Many can't tell profound insight from clever sounding nonsense. And this isn't just about individual choices anymore. Structural forces now shape how ideas spread. and they increasingly work against the deep, difficult thinking human flourishing needs. We're not merely choosing dumb ideas. We're becoming the kind of creatures who can't help but choose them. Still, even now, there's a choice. The herd promises comfort, belonging, and the sweet reassurance of being right alongside everyone else. But Nichzche offered something far rarer. The herd gives you comfort. Freedom of thought gives you meaning. You can stay safe in the herd. Or you can embrace the loneliness and struggle of thinking for yourself. Because in a world where dumb ideas go viral precisely because they're dumb, the most radical act might simply be to think clearly. In a culture that rewards conformity, the greatest rebellion might be to question what everyone else accepts. The herd will always be there to welcome you back. But once you've tasted true independent thought, once you felt the meaning that comes from thinking for yourself, you'll understand why Nichzche believed it was worth any price. So ask yourself, can you afford to think independently? Or more importantly, can you afford not to? Because in the end, the dumbest idea of all is believing someone else can do your thinking for you. And if you know someone who believes every conspiracy that pops up in their feed, or someone who swallows every trending opinion without a second thought, maybe share this with them. Not to prove you're smarter, but because we all need reminders. In an age where going along with the herd is the easiest thing in the world, the real revolution might simply be thinking for yourself.

He waited. Are you sorry the article happened or are you sorry you brought me into a life where the article was always going to happen? His mouth opened. He closed it again. He took a long breath. Both, he said honestly. But the second one most of all, she nodded. Then we need a third option, she said. Not me leaving. Not you protecting me from this by paying me to disappear. A third option where I get to decide what I am to you and you get to decide what you are to me. And we tell that to the world together before they make it up for us. Because I will not, Adrien, be a mystery brunette. I refuse. I am a person. I am a person with a name and a brother and an aunt and a job and a life. And if I am going to be in your life, I am going to be in it as Ren McKenzie. And the world is going to learn how to spell that. And I am not going to spend the rest of this strange and unexpected friendship hiding inside diner booths. He stared at her. And then in the long marble hallway on the 40th floor of his own building, Adrienne Howerin laughed. It was a real laugh. It was a shocked, broken open, almost young laugh. It was, Ren realized, the first laugh she had ever heard come out of him. Ren McKenzie, he said. Adrien Howerin, I would like very much to be a person in your life officially on the record with your full name spelled correctly. And I would like also to be the kind of person who can show up at a fundraiser in something other than a borrowed dress because if I show up in a borrowed dress, the tabloids will write that too, and you will be embarrassed for me. and I do not wish to be the source of any further embarrassment to you ever. She looked at him steadily. Then we'll buy a dress, one dress with my consultancy paycheck, not yours. And we will go to a fundraiser together, and you will introduce me by name, and you will say what I do for the foundation, and you will not under any circumstances behave as if I am someone you are sneaking. Is that understood? Yes, ma'am, he said. His voice was rough. I will not be embarrassed of you. I will not be embarrassed of my brother, of my aunt, of where I live, of where I work, of any single thing about my life. And if you, Adrien, at any point feel embarrassed of any of those things, then you will tell me immediately and I will go back to cleaning your floors at night, and we will both pretend none of this ever happened. I will never, he said, be embarrassed of any single thing about you. Then we have a plan, Ren said. They sat in silence for another moment. Then Adrienne Hollerin said very quietly almost shily. Ren, "Yes, Henry would have liked you," she smiled. She felt her eyes sting. "I would have liked him too," she said. "Tell me again about the bear book." The fundraiser was 3 weeks later. Ren wore a dark green dress she had bought herself at a sample sale in the garment district. And she wore the only pair of heels she owned, and she pinned her hair up with her grandmother's silver comb, and she walked into a ballroom full of women in jewelry that cost more than her building, and she did not, for a single moment, flinch. Adrienne introduced her by name at every table. This is Ren McKenzie, who is helping us rebuild the Henry Howerin Foundation from the inside out. Some of them shook her hand warmly. Some of them shook her hand coolly. One of them, a thin woman in pearl gray with a face like a closed door, looked at her and said without bothering to lower her voice that it was so wonderful that Adrienne was finally giving back to the community. Ren smiled the way she had learned to smile at 26 years old in a thousand rooms where she had not been wanted. And she said very pleasantly that Adrienne was not the one giving back, that the foundation was, and that the foundation belonged to the families it served, and that she was just very lucky to be allowed to learn from them. The woman in Pearl Gay was, it would later turn out, Adrienne Howerin's mother. Her name was Cordelia. She did not approve. She did not approve of the dark green dress or the silver con or the cleaning job or the fourth floor walk up or the diner where her son had been photographed or the burrows in general. She did not approve in particular of the way Adrien in the middle of his speech at the podium looked across the ballroom at Ren and said into the microphone. I want to thank one person in particular tonight. a person who has reminded me of what this foundation is supposed to be and of what my son's name is supposed to mean. Ren McKenzie, stand up, Ren, please. I will not pretend you are not here." Ren stood. There was scattered applause. Cordelia Howerin did not clap. Ren did not care. She sat back down. After the fundraiser, when the cars were lining up at the valet, Cordelia caught her arm. "A word, my dear," she said. They stepped aside under the awning in the cold. Cordelia's hand was bony and cold and waited with one enormous ring. "You seem like a very practical young woman," Cordelia said quietly. "So, I will be practical with you." "My son has been through more than any human being should bear. He is fragile. He is not currently in his right mind. He latches on to things and people when he is grieving and he will discard them again when he is not. I have seen it happen before. I have watched two of his marriages collapse this way. I am therefore going to make you an offer and I am going to make it once and I am going to expect a yes or a no by the end of this week. I will pay you in cash a sum that will allow your brother to attend a private school of your choosing and your aunt to retire comfortably in exchange for your departure from my son's life. You will resign from the foundation. You will return to your former job with a glowing reference. You will keep the cash. We will all agree privately and amicably that this was the right and humane decision for everyone involved. She named the sum. The sum was so large that Ren felt the breath leave her body in one cold gust. Cordelia Howerin patted her arm. "Take a few days," she said. "I am sure you will see reason." She walked away. Ren stood under the awning alone in the dark green dress with the city loud and indifferent around her. And she did not cry. She did not move. She thought about her brother and his school shoes. She thought about her aunt's swollen feet. She thought about the letter from the property management company which had been followed in the month since by a second letter and a third. She thought then about Henry's small face in the photograph and about the way Adrienne had said, "Would you say his name, please, just once?" And she thought with a clarity so cold and so bright it almost hurt that there were two kinds of women in this world. There were the women who took the money and there were the women who did not. And Ren McKenzie, 26 years old, daughter of a woman who had died too young in a bed too narrow, sister of a boy who slept in a bunk bed in a cracked apartment. niece of a woman who had cleaned other people's houses for 30 years and had still never ever sold one piece of her dignity, had been raised by all three of those women to be the second kind. She walked in her green dress and her tired heels out from under the awning. And she found Adrien by the curb and she put her arm through his in front of every person standing on that sidewalk. And she said clearly so that anyone who wanted to could hear it, "Take me home, please, to my apartment where I live with my family." And he did. She told him about the offer the next morning. she told him in his kitchen, sitting on a tall stool at the marble island in his penthouse, while he scrambled eggs with the careful focus of a man who had only recently learned to scramble eggs, and was determined to perform the task with dignity. She told him in flat sentences, without embellishment, without performance. She told him the sum. He set down the spatula. He did not turn around. For a long moment, he stood with his back to her, his shoulders very still, his head bowed slightly toward the pan. Then, very quietly, in a voice she had not heard from him before, he said, "She is my mother, and I love her, and I will never for the rest of either of our lives forgive her for this." Ren watched him. Adrien. He turned around. His eyes were dry, but his face was so tired that she could see suddenly and clearly the man he was going to be at 60. "I am going to call her tonight," he said. "I am going to tell her with witnesses that she is not to contact you again and that she is not to attempt to negotiate the terms of your presence in my life ever again and that if she does, she will lose access to me entirely. I will be very calm. I will be very polite and I will be very completely irreversibly clear. Do you understand? Ren nodded. And then he said, I am going to ask you something. Not today. Not this week. Not until I have been the kind of man in this kitchen and in that office and at every fundraiser between here and Christmas who has earned the right to ask it. But I want you to know now in advance that I am going to ask it. I am telling you that I am going to ask it so that you have months if you want them to prepare your answer. I do not want to surprise you. I do not want you to feel cornered. I want you to have from this morning forward the full and considered freedom to know what is coming and to think it through with your aunt and your brother and yourself and to decide what you want on your own terms in your own time with no pressure from me at all. Do you know what I am telling you? Ren's chest was very full. She nodded once. I know, she said. Good, he said. He turned back to the eggs. He served them to her on a plain white plate with one piece of toast slightly burned at the edge and one piece of bacon that had crisped a little too much. She ate every bite of it. It was the best breakfast she had ever eaten in her life. He drove her home himself afterward. He met Theo at the door. He shook her brother's hand gravely as if Theo were a man of consequence. He sat at her aunt's kitchen table for an hour, drinking instant coffee that he had never in his life had a reason to drink. And at the end of that hour, her aunt Alda, who had not been impressed by a single man in 30 years, looked across the table at him and said in her dry, careful voice, "When you marry her, I expect to be the one who cooks the wedding food." None of this catering business. The cooks will be from this kitchen or there will be no wedding. Adrien Howerin, the most powerful real estate developer in the city, nodded once very gravely. "Yes, ma'am," he said. "If she has me, the food will be from this kitchen." Emldda nodded back. Theo, who was seven, said, "Are you going to be my brother?" Adrien thought about this very seriously. I would like very much, he said, to be your friend first and then, if your sister allows it one day, to be your brother. Is that all right with you? Theo considered. Will you bring more coloring books? I will bring all the coloring books you can color, Adrienne said. Then, yes, said Theo. Alda hid a smile in her coffee. Ren on the other side of the table looked at the three of them and felt the room go warm around her in a way that no rich man's penthouse had ever made her feel. 6 months later, in a small church across the street from her aunt's apartment building with 32 people in attendance and the food on the buffet entirely made by Alda and three of her sisters. Ren McKenzie married Adrienne Howerin. She wore the same green dress she had worn to the fundraiser because she had not been raised to throw away good dresses. She wore her grandmother's silver con. She walked herself down the aisle because there was no one in her life who had the right to give her away, and she had already herself given the part of her she was willing to give. Adrienne was waiting at the altar. He cried. the new senior community liaison from the Henry Howerin Foundation, a young father from a family the foundation had served, conducted the ceremony. Theo was the ring bearer. Emldda did not cry, but at one point she pressed her hand very hard against her own mouth, and that was almost the same thing. Cordelia Howerin did not attend. She had not in the end accepted that her son was building his life around a woman in a green dress from a sample sale. Ren did not have the energy to be wounded by the absence. She had her family. They moved eventually into a building Adrienne owned, but they moved into a regular two-bedroom unit on a regular floor, not the penthouse. Ren refused the penthouse. The penthouse, she said, was where his old life had lived. They needed a place that had never been anyone's life before. They got Theo into a good school in the neighborhood. They paid for it themselves out of Ren's foundation salary and Adrienne's regular paycheck. They did not touch the family money. They lived by the standards of Adrienne's world modestly. By Ren's standards, they lived in a kind of careful, watchful abundance she had to talk herself into every morning by reminding herself that her brother now slept in a room with a window that did not look out onto a brick wall. The foundation grew. It grew because Ren built it from the inside the way she had built everything in her life. By getting up at 6:00 in the morning and showing up and asking the right questions of the right people in the right rooms, it grew because Adrien, for the first time in his life, was allowed to say his son's name out loud every day in front of strangers without coming apart. He still cried at certain anniversaries. He cried on Henry's birthday every single year on the floor of his office at 1:53 in the morning. And Ren, who knew would always go to him, and they would sit together 10 ft apart on the carpet, and she would say in her voice that was steady and soft and warm and absolutely her own, the name Henry, and he would cry and breathe and breathe and rebuild. Years later, after their own daughter was born, and they named her McKenzie Henrietta Howerin, after the boy and the woman whose name had carried him through the worst night of his life, Ren would sometimes wake up in the middle of the night and walk to the window and look out at the city he owned so much of, and she would think about the woman she had been on the bus that night with the property management letter in her back pocket and her hand throbbing where she had twisted it on a mop bucket. And she would think about how thin the line is in this world between the people who have everything and the people who have nothing. And she would think about how sometimes all it takes to cross that line in either direction is to be the person willing to stop in a hallway and listen just for one second to a sound on the other side of a door.
